extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification enables one skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue (unreasonable) experimentation, including how claim scope, examples, and known art affect enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of Enablement (undue experimentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the disclosure, when filed, contained sufficient information regarding the subject matter of the claims as to enable one skilled in the pertinent art to make and use the claimed invention; cast as whether the experimentation needed to practice the invention is undue or unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Minerals Separation/Hyde formulation and related precedent (e.g., In re Wands; United States v. Telectronics): the proper test is whether a person reasonably skilled in the art could make or use the invention from the patent disclosures plus knowledge in the art without undue experimentation. The specification need not teach what is well known in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Wands factors to assess undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess enablement by considering the Wands factors (as developed in In re Wands) to determine whether required experimentation is undue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP directs use of the Wands factors regardless of technology. Amgen did not displace Wands; see also Guidelines for Assessing Enablement (89 FR 1563, Jan 10, 2024). For further discussion of quantity/reasonableness of experimentation see MPEP §2164.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of experimentation — reasonableness depends on invention and art
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation; what is reasonable depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex experimentation does not automatically make experimentation undue if the art typically engages in such work (e.g., cell culture work). The test is not whether any experimentation is necessary, but whether necessary experimentation is undue (see In re Angstadt). See MPEP §2164.06 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claim vs enablement (broader claims require broader enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent claims an entire class (genus) of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class; 'the more one claims, the more one must enable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amgen (2023) applied this principle to invalidated genus antibody claims that were defined functionally; broader functional/genus claims will require disclosure enabling the full scope. The specification does not always need to describe every embodiment, but broader claim scope increases the disclosure burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claiming and risk of non-enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionally defined genus claims (claims defined by result or function rather than structure) are at risk of failing enablement if the specification does not adequately enable the full scope of the claimed functionally-defined class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Amgen's claims to a genus of antibodies defined by binding function were found not to enable the full scope. Functional claiming without structural or enabling guidance across the genus can render claims invalid for lack of enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples plus general quality disclosure may suffice for genus enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A few examples can suffice to enable a claimed class if the specification also discloses some general quality running through the class that gives it a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose, thereby reliably enabling the full class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not describe with particularity every embodiment if it discloses general qualities or principles that reliably enable the class. However, courts will evaluate whether those examples and generalizations truly enable the full claimed scope (Amgen discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may omit well-known art
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent need not teach, and preferably omits, what is well known in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner/practitioner should not require disclosure of conventional or routine matters known to one of ordinary skill. See In re Buchner and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any part of the specification can supply enabling disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Any portion of the specification, including background sections that discuss or disparage subject matter, can support an enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discount background or critical discussion as non-enabling; such portions may nevertheless teach how to make and use features (Callicrate). Statements disparaging prior art do not mean one of ordinary skill would not know how to make/use the feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement is a legal determination based on underlying factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether a disclosure is enabling is a question of law that is based on underlying factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply factual inquiries (e.g., what a person of ordinary skill knows, what the specification discloses, the nature of required experimentation) and then reach the legal conclusion on enablement (see In re Vaeck; Atlas Powder).
